title: Public meeting on 1 Clair Road East towers
subtitle: Parkland fee exemption for home additions, a Woolwich Street apartment unit, and a closed-session land item.
overview: Council held the statutory public meeting on a proposal to redevelop part of the Pergola Commons plaza at 1 Clair Road East with four mixed-use buildings and five towers of 10 to 14 storeys, 715 homes and about 2,127 square metres of ground-floor commercial space. Council only received the report {{vote:m2}}. No decision on the Official Plan and zoning changes was made, and staff will bring a recommendation report to a later meeting.

Residents who spoke raised traffic on Poppy Drive, parking, density, and the loss of the cinema and other businesses. Councillors asked about commercial space, parking, phasing and building variety, and staff took several questions away.

Council also changed the Parkland Dedication By-law so that additions or alterations to homes that add no units no longer trigger parkland or cash-in-lieu charges. It exempted a single new bachelor unit at 671 Woolwich Street from a fee staff estimated at about $112,000 {{vote:m4}}. After a closed session, the mayor reported that council received information and gave staff direction on the Hanlon Creek land disposition.

decisions.detail: Council received the statutory public meeting report on the proposed Official Plan and zoning amendments for 715 homes in towers of 10 to 14 storeys {{vote:m2}}, with no decision on the application yet.
Council amended the by-law so additions or alterations to residential buildings that create no new units or change of use no longer require parkland conveyance or cash-in-lieu {{vote:m4}}.
The same motion authorized a building permit for one added bachelor unit at 671 Woolwich Street without the cash-in-lieu of parkland payment otherwise required.

debate: Delegates and callers opposed or questioned the scale of the proposal, citing traffic and parking on Poppy Drive and nearby streets, waste collection problems, school capacity, and the effect of adding five tall towers. One resident asked for deferral, a redesign or a cumulative impact study.

Several residents and councillors worried about losing commercial space and community amenities, including the cinema and fitness facility. The applicant said commercial space on the redevelopment site would be about half of what exists today and that a commercial function study was filed. It said the cinema's lease must be respected and the new space is not sized for a theatre.

Councillors pressed on parking and timing. The applicant said visitor and commercial parking would be a shared pool, and EV-ready spaces were not proposed at this stage. It could not give a build-out timeline because of existing leases and market conditions. One councillor suggested lowering the height to meet parking minimums; another wished for taller buildings so more commercial space could stay.

Councillors asked about vehicle access from the pedestrian-focused street to Poppy Drive and the alignment with the Tricar access. Staff said they would report back on this and on Poppy Drive capacity. Staff also pointed to the Gordon Street environmental assessment, which began in April.

On parkland, staff said the fee for home additions is hard to administer and the single-unit fee of about $112,000 was out of proportion. A planning consultant for the Woolwich Street property owner supported the exemption. Another delegate backed the by-law change and raised a separate fee timing concern, which council directed toward the petition process.
